title: Ἀγήνωρ
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Artemis, weeping, comes to Olympus and sits on Zeus’ knees; he asks who hurt her, and she blames Hera. Apollo goes into Troy to guard the wall, and the other gods go up to Olympus, some angry and some glorying. Achilles goes on killing, and Priam, watching from the tower, has the gates opened for the fleeing Trojans and ordered shut again once they are in. Apollo rouses Agenor, who stands his ground before the city. He weighs flight against a stand, compares himself to a leopard, taunts Achilles and throws his spear, but Achilles’ armour, a god’s gift, turns it. When Achilles rushes at him, Apollo snatches him away in mist and lures Achilles over the plain towards the Scamander in Agenor’s shape, while the Trojans pour into the city.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, Λητὼ δὲ συναίνυτο καμπύλα τόξα
πεπτεῶτ’ ἄλλυδις ἄλλα μετὰ στροφάλιγγι κονίης.
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, Lētō de synainyto kampyla toxa
pepteōt’ allydis alla meta strophalingi koniēs.
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and Leto gathered up the bent bows
fallen, some here, some there, in the whirl of dust.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Leto gathered up the bent bows that lay scattered here and there in the whirl of dust.
sentences.n: Hermes’ speech to Leto closed at the end of the last part, and ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη ‘so then he spoke’ rounds it off. Artemis, who has fled weeping, is not named here; the bows are hers. συναίνυτο is the imperfect of συναίνυμαι ‘gather up’. τόξα is the plural of τόξον ‘bow’; Homer often uses it for one bow, but ἄλλυδις ἄλλα ‘some this way, some that’ asks for more than one thing, so the English keeps the plural, ‘bent bows’. πεπτεῶτ’ is the perfect participle of πίπτω (Attic πεπτωκότα), ‘fallen’, and στροφάλιγγι κονίης is ‘in the whirl of dust’.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν τόξα λαβοῦσα πάλιν κίε θυγατέρος ἧς·
sentences.tr: hē men toxa labousa palin kie thygateros hēs·
sentences.l: She, on the one hand, having taken her own daughter’s bows, went back;
sentences.i: She took up her own daughter’s bows and went back;
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν ‘she for her part’ is Leto, and the ἣ δ’ of the next unit turns to the other, Artemis. κίε is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’. θυγατέρος ἧς is ‘of her own daughter’, a genitive that hangs on τόξα ‘bows’ across the verb (the bows are Artemis’s, as at 502), not a goal after κίε; where Leto goes the poet does not say. ἧς is the possessive ‘her own’, not the relative. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted, at its end: scanning it needs a lengthened syllable in θυγατέρος (fifth foot) and the old digamma of ἧς to make the syllable before it long (sixth foot).

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄρ’ Ὄλυμπον ἵκανε Διὸς ποτὶ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ,
δακρυόεσσα δὲ πατρὸς ἐφέζετο γούνασι κούρη,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀμβρόσιος ἑανὸς τρέμε·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ar’ Olympon hikane Dios poti chalkobates dō,
dakryoessa de patros ephezeto gounasi kourē,
amphi d’ ar’ ambrosios heanos treme·
sentences.i: She came to Olympus, to the house of Zeus with the bronze floor, and the maiden sat tearful upon her father’s knees, and her fine, ambrosial robe trembled about her;
sentences.n: Artemis reaches Olympus; the poet still calls her only ‘the maiden’ (κούρη), and Zeus is named only in the genitive Διός. ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come’. δῶ is δῶμα ‘house’, and whether χαλκοβατές means a bronze floor or a bronze threshold is disputed; the house rendering is ‘the bronze-floored house’. ἐφέζετο ‘sat down upon’ takes the dative γούνασι ‘knees’, and δακρυόεσσα is ‘tearful’. ἑανός is a fine robe, but the exact sense of the word is not known. τρέμε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘trembled’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ προτὶ οἷ
εἷλε πατὴρ Κρονίδης, καὶ ἀνείρετο ἡδὺ γελάσσας·
sentences.tr:
tēn de proti hoi
heile patēr Kronidēs, kai aneireto hēdy gelassas·
sentences.l:
and her to himself
took her father, the son of Cronus, and questioned, having laughed sweetly:
sentences.i: Her father, the son of Cronus, drew her to him and, laughing sweetly, questioned her:
sentences.n: Zeus draws his daughter to him. εἷλε is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, and with προτὶ οἷ (προτί = πρός, οἷ ‘to himself’) it means ‘took her to himself’. πατὴρ Κρονίδης is ‘the father, the son of Cronus’, which is Zeus. ἀνείρετο (= Attic ἀνήρετο) is ‘questioned’, and ἡδὺ γελάσσας ‘having laughed sweetly’ is an aorist participle with an adverbial accusative. His words follow.

sentences.t:
τίς νύ σε τοιάδ’ ἔρεξε φίλον τέκος Οὐρανιώνων
μαψιδίως, ὡς εἴ τι κακὸν ῥέζουσαν ἐνωπῇ;
sentences.tr:
tis ny se toiad’ erexe philon tekos Ouraniōnōn
mapsidiōs, hōs ei ti kakon rhezousan enōpēi;
sentences.l:
“Who then of the Uranians has done such things to you, dear child,
without cause, as if you were doing some evil openly?”
sentences.i: “Which of the gods of heaven has done such things to you, dear child, without cause, as if you were doing some evil in the open?”
sentences.n: Zeus asks his daughter who has done this. The two lines are word for word those Dione speaks to the wounded Aphrodite at 5.373–374, and the English is the same. τίς … Οὐρανιώνων is ‘which of the Uranians’: the Οὐρανίωνες, descendants of Οὐρανός ‘Heaven’, are the gods of heaven, in the genitive plural, with the vocative φίλον τέκος ‘dear child’ set between. νύ is ‘then’, τοιάδ’ is τοιάδε ‘such things’, and ἔρεξε is the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’. μαψιδίως is ‘without cause’. ὡς εἴ τι κακὸν ῥέζουσαν is ‘as if you were doing some evil’, the participle agreeing with σε ‘you’, and ἐνωπῇ is ‘openly, in plain sight’. The question mark is the Greek semicolon.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἐϋστέφανος κελαδεινή·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen eÿstephanos keladeinē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the fair-crowned, the resounding:
sentences.i: Then the fair-crowned, resounding one spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Artemis answers, named only by her epithets. τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν is the whole-line formula ‘then … spoke to him in turn’: τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπεν the uncontracted epic aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’. ἐϋστέφανος ‘fair-crowned’ (ἐΰ ‘well’ + στέφανος ‘crown’) and κελαδεινή ‘resounding’ (from κελαδέω ‘make a loud noise’; what it is that sounds is not said) are epithets translated every time, and here they stand for her name. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
σή μ’ ἄλοχος στυφέλιξε πάτερ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
ἐξ ἧς ἀθανάτοισιν ἔρις καὶ νεῖκος ἐφῆπται.
sentences.tr:
sē m’ alochos styphelixe pater leukōlenos Hērē,
ex hēs athanatoisin eris kai neikos ephēptai.
sentences.l:
“Your wife thrust me roughly, father, white-armed Hera,
because of whom upon the immortals strife and quarrel have been fastened.”
sentences.i: “Your wife shoved me, father, white-armed Hera, because of whom strife and quarrel have been fastened upon the immortals.”
sentences.n: Artemis names her attacker. σή is ‘your’ (possessive σός) with ἄλοχος ‘wife’, and the name Ἥρη is held back to the end of the line, after the address πάτερ ‘father’. στυφέλιξε is the aorist of στυφελίζω ‘thrust roughly’, ‘shove’. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is the epithet of Hera, translated every time. ἐφῆπται is the perfect passive of ἐφάπτω ‘fasten upon’, with the dative ἀθανάτοισιν ‘upon the immortals’ and the two subjects ἔρις ‘strife’ and νεῖκος ‘quarrel’. In ἐξ ἧς the ἧς is the relative ‘whom’, not the possessive: the strife comes ‘from’ Hera.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon·
sentences.l: So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking;
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another;
sentences.n: The poet closes the scene on Olympus with Zeus and his daughter. ὣς οἳ μέν looks forward to the αὐτάρ of the next unit, which turns to Apollo. ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’, and πρὸς ἀλλήλους is ‘to one another’. The line also stands at 5.274. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Ἀπόλλων Φοῖβος ἐδύσετο Ἴλιον ἱρήν·
sentences.tr: autar Apollōn Phoibos edyseto Ilion hirēn·
sentences.l: but Apollo Phoebus entered sacred Ilium;
sentences.i: but Phoebus Apollo went into sacred Ilium;
sentences.n: The scene shifts to Troy. αὐτάρ ‘but’ answers the μέν of the line before. ἐδύσετο is an epic aorist of δύομαι ‘enter’ (a by-form of ἐδύσατο). Ἴλιον ἱρήν is ‘sacred Ilium’, ἱρός being the epic spelling of ἱερός.

sentences.t:
μέμβλετο γάρ οἱ τεῖχος ἐϋδμήτοιο πόληος
μὴ Δαναοὶ πέρσειαν ὑπὲρ μόρον ἤματι κείνῳ.
sentences.tr:
membleto gar hoi teichos eÿdmētoio polēos
mē Danaoi perseian hyper moron ēmati keinōi.
sentences.l:
for was a care to him the wall of the well-built city,
lest the Danaans sack it beyond portion on that day.
sentences.i: for the wall of the well-built city was a care to him, lest the Danaans sack it, beyond what was allotted, on that day.
sentences.n: The reason Apollo goes in. μέμβλετο is ‘was a care to’ (from μέλω), with οἱ ‘to him’ and the subject τεῖχος ‘the wall’. μή with the optative πέρσειαν (aorist optative of πέρθω ‘sack’) gives the fear: ‘lest they sack it’. ὑπὲρ μόρον ‘beyond portion’ means beyond what was allotted, that is beyond what is fated (μόρος is one’s allotted share, often a doom); the poet does not say here what that is. The Danaans are named, as the poet chose. ἐϋδμήτοιο is ‘well-built’, with the genitive -οιο (= -ου).

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι πρὸς Ὄλυμπον ἴσαν θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες,
οἳ μὲν χωόμενοι, οἳ δὲ μέγα κυδιόωντες·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alloi pros Olympon isan theoi aien eontes,
hoi men chōomenoi, hoi de mega kydioōntes·
sentences.l:
And the others, to Olympus went, the gods who are forever,
some angered, others greatly glorying;
sentences.i: The other gods, who are forever, went to Olympus, some angry, others glorying greatly;
sentences.n: The gods return to Olympus. οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι ‘and the others’ are the other gods, who had been fighting one another. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (= ᾔεσαν). θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες ‘the gods who are forever’ is a formula, translated the same way each time. οἳ μὲν … οἳ δὲ ‘some … others’ divides them into the angry and the exultant, and the poet does not say which gods are which. χωόμενοι is the present participle of χώομαι ‘be angry’, and κυδιόωντες (from κυδιάω) ‘glorying’ comes from κῦδος ‘glory’.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἷζον παρὰ πατρὶ κελαινεφεῖ·
sentences.tr: kad d’ hizon para patri kelainephei·
sentences.l: and down they sat beside their father, the dark-clouded;
sentences.i: and they sat down beside their father, of the dark clouds;
sentences.n: κὰδ … ἷζον is tmesis: κάδ (= κατά, with its last letter taken into the following δ) stands apart from ἷζον, and together they mean ‘sat down’ (καθίζω). ἷζον is the imperfect of ἵζω. The father is Zeus, who is not named; κελαινεφής ‘dark-clouded’ (‘of the dark clouds’ in the English) is his epithet, translated every time. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
Τρῶας ὁμῶς αὐτούς τ’ ὄλεκεν καὶ μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
Trōas homōs autous t’ oleken kai mōnychas hippous.
sentences.l:
but Achilles
was destroying the Trojans alike, themselves and the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: while Achilles went on killing the Trojans, men and solid-hoofed horses alike.
sentences.n: Back on the plain. ὄλεκεν is the unaugmented imperfect of ὀλέκω ‘destroy, kill’, a slaughter that goes on. αὐτούς ‘themselves’ sets the men over against the horses, and ὁμῶς … τε καὶ is ‘alike … both … and’. μώνυχας ἵππους ‘solid-hoofed horses’ is a stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε καπνὸς ἰὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἵκηται
ἄστεος αἰθομένοιο, θεῶν δέ ἑ μῆνις ἀνῆκε,
πᾶσι δ’ ἔθηκε πόνον, πολλοῖσι δὲ κήδε’ ἐφῆκεν,
ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς Τρώεσσι πόνον καὶ κήδε’ ἔθηκεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote kapnos iōn eis ouranon euryn hikētai
asteos aithomenoio, theōn de he mēnis anēke,
pasi d’ ethēke ponon, polloisi de kēde’ ephēken,
hōs Achileus Trōessi ponon kai kēde’ ethēken.
sentences.l:
And as when smoke, going to broad heaven, arrives,
of a burning town, and the wrath of the gods has sent it up,
and for all has laid toil, and on many has sent sorrows,
so Achilles on the Trojans laid toil and sorrows.
sentences.i: As when smoke goes up to the broad heaven from a burning town, and the wrath of the gods has sent it up, and has laid toil on all and sent sorrows upon many, so Achilles laid toil and sorrows on the Trojans.
sentences.n: A simile: Achilles is to the Trojans as the gods’ wrath is to the people of a burning town. ὡς δ’ ὅτε … ὣς … is ‘as when … so …’, the comparison closing at 525. ἵκηται is a subjunctive without κε, as is usual in similes; ἰών is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. ἄστεος αἰθομένοιο ‘of a burning town’ is a genitive after καπνός ‘smoke’. ἀνῆκε is the aorist of ἀνίημι, here ‘sent up’; whether ἑ ‘it’ is the smoke or the town the Greek does not say, so ‘it’ stands. πόνος is ‘toil’ and κήδεα ‘sorrows’. In 525 Ἀχιλεύς has a single λ for the metre.

sentences.t:
ἑστήκει δ’ ὃ γέρων Πρίαμος θείου ἐπὶ πύργου,
ἐς δ’ ἐνόησ’ Ἀχιλῆα πελώριον·
sentences.tr:
hestēkei d’ ho gerōn Priamos theiou epi pyrgou,
es d’ enoēs’ Achilēa pelōrion·
sentences.l:
And was standing the old man Priam upon the divine tower,
and he perceived Achilles, huge;
sentences.i: Old Priam was standing on the divine tower, and he perceived huge Achilles;
sentences.n: A new scene, on the wall of Troy. ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘was standing’ (Attic ἑστήκει), and ὃ γέρων is ‘the old man’, ὁ in its Homeric use as a pointing ‘the’. θείου is ‘divine’. ἐς … ἐνόησ’ is tmesis for εἰσενόησε ‘perceived, caught sight of’. πελώριον ‘huge’ is the house rendering, a word of wonder here and not of dread.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ
Τρῶες ἄφαρ κλονέοντο πεφυζότες, οὐδέ τις ἀλκὴ
γίγνεθ’·
sentences.tr:
autar hyp’ autou
Trōes aphar kloneonto pephyzotes, oude tis alkē
gigneth’·
sentences.i: and under his onslaught the Trojans were at once thrown into confusion, in flight, and no might arose among them;
sentences.n: What Priam sees. ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘under him’ is the pressure of Achilles on them. κλονέοντο is the uncontracted passive imperfect of κλονέω, ‘were being thrown into confusion’, and πεφυζότες is a perfect participle of a verb ‘to flee in panic’ (related to φύζα ‘rout’), ‘put to flight’. ἄφαρ is ‘at once’. ἀλκή is ‘might’, and γίγνεθ’ is γίγνετο elided (the τ turns to θ before the rough breathing of the next word), the imperfect ‘was coming to be, arose’; the sentence runs on into the next line and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ οἰμώξας ἀπὸ πύργου βαῖνε χαμᾶζε
ὀτρύνων παρὰ τεῖχος ἀγακλειτοὺς πυλαωρούς·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ oimōxas apo pyrgou baine chamaze
otrynōn para teichos agakleitous pylaōrous·
sentences.l:
and he, groaning, from the tower went down to the ground,
urging along the wall the renowned gatekeepers:
sentences.i: and with a groan he went down from the tower to the ground, urging on the renowned gatekeepers along the wall:
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Priam. οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω ‘groan, wail’. βαῖνε is the unaugmented imperfect of βαίνω ‘go’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ has the old suffix -ζε (= -δε) of motion towards. ὀτρύνων is ‘urging’, παρὰ τεῖχος ‘along the wall’. ἀγακλειτούς ‘renowned’ and πυλαωρούς ‘gatekeepers’ (from πύλη ‘gate’) agree. The unit ends at an ano teleia and his speech follows.

sentences.t:
πεπταμένας ἐν χερσὶ πύλας ἔχετ’ εἰς ὅ κε λαοὶ
ἔλθωσι προτὶ ἄστυ πεφυζότες·
sentences.tr:
peptamenas en chersi pylas echet’ eis ho ke laoi
elthōsi proti asty pephyzotes·
sentences.l:
“Hold the gates, spread open, in your hands, until the people
come to the town, put to flight;
sentences.i: “Keep the gates standing open in your hands until the troops have come to the town in their flight;
sentences.n: Priam gives his orders to the gatekeepers. ἔχετ’ is the plural imperative of ἔχω ‘hold’, with πύλας ‘gates’ and πεπταμένας, the perfect passive participle of πετάννυμι ‘spread open’, so ‘hold the gates opened’; ἐν χερσίν is ‘in your hands’. εἰς ὅ κε with the aorist subjunctive ἔλθωσι is ‘until they come’. λαοί ‘people’ are the Trojan troops, προτὶ ἄστυ is ‘to the town’ (προτί = πρός), and πεφυζότες ‘put to flight’ is the word of 528.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐγγὺς ὅδε κλονέων·
sentences.tr:
ē gar Achilleus
engys hode kloneōn·
sentences.l:
for truly Achilles
is near, here, throwing them into confusion;
sentences.i: for Achilles is here, close by, throwing them into confusion;
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. ὅδε ‘this one here’ is Achilles as Priam sees him, and ἐγγύς is ‘near’. κλονέων is the present participle of κλονέω used transitively, ‘throwing (them) into confusion’, where 528 had the passive.

sentences.t: νῦν οἴω λοίγι’ ἔσεσθαι.
sentences.tr: nyn oiō loigi’ esesthai.
sentences.l: now I think there will be ruin-bringing things.
sentences.i: I think now there will be disaster.
sentences.n: οἴω is οἴομαι ‘I think’ in its short Homeric form, with the future infinitive ἔσεσθαι ‘will be’. λοίγια is the neuter plural of λοίγιος ‘ruin-bringing’, from λοιγός ‘ruin’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ἐς τεῖχος ἀναπνεύσωσιν ἀλέντες,
αὖτις ἐπανθέμεναι σανίδας πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας·
δείδια γὰρ μὴ οὖλος ἀνὴρ ἐς τεῖχος ἅληται.
sentences.tr:
autar epei k’ es teichos anapneusōsin alentes,
autis epanthemenai sanidas pykinōs araruias·
deidia gar mē oulos anēr es teichos halētai.
sentences.i: But when they have got their breath back inside the wall, crowded together, put the closely fitted doors on again; for I fear that the ruinous man may leap into the wall.”
sentences.n: The order to shut the gates again. ἐπεί κ’ … ἀναπνεύσωσιν is ‘when they have recovered their breath’, an aorist subjunctive with κε (= ἄν). ἀλέντες is the aorist passive participle of εἴλω, ‘crowded, huddled together’. ἐπανθέμεναι ‘put on again’ is an infinitive standing for a command, with σανίδας, literally ‘boards’ and here the doors of the gates, and πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας, a perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, ‘closely fitted’. δείδια is the perfect of δείδω ‘fear’, with μή and the aorist subjunctive ἅληται of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’. οὖλος ‘ruinous’ is Achilles, who is not named. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄνεσάν τε πύλας καὶ ἀπῶσαν ὀχῆας·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ anesan te pylas kai apōsan ochēas·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they both opened the gates and thrust back the bolts;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they opened the gates and thrust back the bolts;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ is the formula that closes a speech. ἄνεσαν is the aorist of ἀνίημι, which with πύλας ‘gates’ is ‘threw open’, and ἀπῶσαν (= ἀπέωσαν) is the aorist of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust away’, with ὀχῆας ‘bolts’. ἄνεσάν τε … καὶ is ‘both … and’. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t: αἳ δὲ πετασθεῖσαι τεῦξαν φάος·
sentences.tr: hai de petastheisai teuxan phaos·
sentences.l: and they, spread wide, made light;
sentences.i: and the gates, thrown wide, brought light;
sentences.n: αἳ δὲ ‘and they’ are the gates (πύλαι are feminine). πετασθεῖσαι is the aorist passive participle of πετάννυμι ‘spread open’, and τεῦξαν the aorist of τεύχω ‘make’. φάος is ‘light’, and in Homer it can also mean ‘relief, deliverance’; both senses fit the Trojans streaming in.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀπόλλων
ἀντίος ἐξέθορε Τρώων ἵνα λοιγὸν ἀλάλκοι.
sentences.tr:
autar Apollōn
antios exethore Trōōn hina loigon alalkoi.
sentences.l:
but Apollo
sprang out in front of him, that from the Trojans ruin he might keep away.
sentences.i: but Apollo sprang out to face him, to keep ruin away from the Trojans.
sentences.n: Apollo, who went into the city at 515, now comes out to meet Achilles. ἐξέθορε is the aorist of ἐκθρῴσκω ‘leap out’, and ἀντίος is ‘facing’. ἵνα with the optative ἀλάλκοι is ‘in order that he might keep away’, with λοιγόν ‘ruin’ as its object and Τρώων ‘from the Trojans’ as a genitive of separation.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἰθὺς πόλιος καὶ τείχεος ὑψηλοῖο
δίψῃ καρχαλέοι κεκονιμένοι ἐκ πεδίοιο
φεῦγον·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ithys polios kai teicheos hypsēloio
dipsēi karchaleoi kekonimenoi ek pedioio
pheugon·
sentences.i: And they, parched with thirst and covered with dust, fled from the plain straight for the city and its high wall;
sentences.n: The Trojans in flight. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’. ἰθύς ‘straight’ takes the genitives πόλιος καὶ τείχεος (the old forms of πόλεως, τείχους) and ὑψηλοῖο (-οιο = -ου). δίψῃ is the dative ‘with thirst’, and καρχαλέοι ‘parched’ is a rare word whose sense is the traditional one. κεκονιμένοι is the perfect passive participle of κονίω ‘cover with dust’. φεῦγον is an imperfect without augment.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ σφεδανὸν ἔφεπ’ ἔγχεϊ, λύσσα δέ οἱ κῆρ
αἰὲν ἔχε κρατερή, μενέαινε δὲ κῦδος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ho de sphedanon ephep’ encheï, lyssa de hoi kēr
aien eche kraterē, meneaine de kydos aresthai.
sentences.l:
and he, furiously, went after them with his spear, and frenzy his heart
always held, strong, and he was eager to win glory.
sentences.i: and he went furiously after them with his spear, and a strong frenzy held his heart always, and he was set on winning glory.
sentences.n: Achilles in pursuit; ὃ δὲ ‘and he’. σφεδανόν is an adverb, ‘furiously’. ἔφεπ’ is ἔφεπε, the imperfect of ἐφέπω ‘go after’, with ἔγχεϊ ‘with his spear’ as a dative of means and no object expressed. λύσσα ‘frenzy’ is the subject, with κῆρ ‘heart’ as object (not the κῆρ ‘death-fate’) and κρατερή ‘strong’; ἔχε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘held’. μενέαινε ‘was eager’ takes κῦδος ἀρέσθαι ‘to win glory’, an aorist infinitive middle of αἴρομαι.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν ὑψίπυλον Τροίην ἕλον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
εἰ μὴ Ἀπόλλων Φοῖβος Ἀγήνορα δῖον ἀνῆκε
φῶτ’ Ἀντήνορος υἱὸν ἀμύμονά τε κρατερόν τε.
sentences.tr:
entha ken hypsipylon Troiēn helon huies Achaiōn,
ei mē Apollōn Phoibos Agēnora dion anēke
phōt’ Antēnoros huion amymona te krateron te.
sentences.i: Then the sons of the Achaeans would have taken high-gated Troy, if Phoebus Apollo had not urged on heavenly Agenor, a man, the son of Antenor, blameless and strong.
sentences.n: Apollo’s help for Troy. ἔνθά κεν … ἕλον is the past unreal, ‘there would have taken’, finished by εἰ μὴ … ἀνῆκε ‘if … had not urged on’. The first line also stands at 16.698. ὑψίπυλον ‘high-gated’ is Troy’s epithet. Ἀγήνορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Agenor’, and φῶτ’ ‘a man’ stands in apposition to him. ἀμύμονα is translated ‘blameless’, but the true sense of ἀμύμων is not known. ἀνῆκε, the aorist of ἀνίημι, is ‘urged on’ here, where at 523 the same verb was ‘sent up’. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t:
ἐν μέν οἱ κραδίῃ θάρσος βάλε, πὰρ δέ οἱ αὐτὸς
ἔστη, ὅπως θανάτοιο βαρείας χεῖρας ἀλάλκοι
φηγῷ κεκλιμένος·
sentences.tr:
en men hoi kradiēi tharsos bale, par de hoi autos
estē, hopōs thanatoio bareias cheiras alalkoi
phēgōi keklimenos·
sentences.i: He cast courage into his heart, and stood beside him himself, to keep the heavy hands of death away, leaning against an oak;
sentences.n: The subject is still Apollo. ἐν … βάλε is tmesis for ‘cast into’, with οἱ ‘him’ and κραδίῃ ‘in his heart’; πὰρ … ἔστη is ‘stood beside’, and αὐτός ‘himself’ means the god in person. ὅπως with the optative ἀλάλκοι is ‘so that he might keep away’, with χεῖρας ‘hands’ as object and θανάτοιο ‘of death’. φηγός is an oak (not the beech of the English name), and κεκλιμένος is the perfect participle of κλίνω ‘lean’, with the dative.

sentences.t: κεκάλυπτο δ’ ἄρ’ ἠέρι πολλῇ.
sentences.tr: kekalypto d’ ar’ ēeri pollēi.
sentences.l: and he was covered, then, in thick mist.
sentences.i: and he was covered in thick mist.
sentences.n: κεκάλυπτο is the pluperfect passive of καλύπτω, ‘had been covered, was covered’; the subject is still Apollo, standing unseen beside Agenor. ἠέρι πολλῇ is ‘thick mist’ (ἀήρ in Homer is mist), and ἄρα ‘then’ marks it as part of the same scene.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ὡς ἐνόησεν Ἀχιλλῆα πτολίπορθον
ἔστη, πολλὰ δέ οἱ κραδίη πόρφυρε μένοντι·
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ hōs enoēsen Achillēa ptoliporthon
estē, polla de hoi kradiē porphyre menonti·
sentences.l:
But he, when he perceived Achilles, the city-sacking,
stood still, and greatly his heart surged within him as he waited;
sentences.i: But when he perceived Achilles, the city-sacker, he stood still, and as he waited his heart surged greatly;
sentences.n: Back to Agenor: ὅ γ’ ‘he’ is Agenor, picked out with γε. ἐνόησεν is ‘perceived’, and πτολίπορθον ‘city-sacking’ is an epithet of Achilles. ἔστη is ‘stood still’. πόρφυρε is the imperfect of πορφύρω ‘surge’, said of the sea and here of the heart. μένοντι is a dative participle agreeing with οἱ ‘to him’, ‘as he waited’, and πολλά is an adverb, ‘greatly’.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr: ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: The poet moves into Agenor’s mind. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed’, εἶπε ‘spoke’, and πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν ‘to his own great-spirited heart’: he addresses his own θυμός, as in a soliloquy, and ὅς is the possessive ‘his own’. The line is word for word 11.403, where Odysseus also speaks to himself in danger. A speech follows.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγών·
sentences.tr: ō moi egōn·
sentences.l: “Oh me;
sentences.i: “Oh me;
sentences.n: Agenor’s soliloquy begins; he weighs three courses in turn: flee with the others, flee another way, stand and fight. ὤ μοι ἐγών is the cry ‘oh me’; ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ, which the English does not render separately. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κεν ὑπὸ κρατεροῦ Ἀχιλῆος
φεύγω, τῇ περ οἱ ἄλλοι ἀτυζόμενοι κλονέονται,
αἱρήσει με καὶ ὧς, καὶ ἀνάλκιδα δειροτομήσει.
sentences.tr:
ei men ken hypo kraterou Achilēos
pheugō, tēi per hoi alloi atyzomenoi kloneontai,
hairēsei me kai hōs, kai analkida deirotomēsei.
sentences.l:
If, to be sure, away from strong Achilles
I flee, where the others, dazed with fear, are being thrown into confusion,
he will take me even so, and cut my throat, without might.
sentences.i: If I flee from strong Achilles, the way the others are being thrown into confusion, dazed with fear, he will catch me all the same and cut the throat of a man with no might.
sentences.n: The first course: flee with the others. εἰ μέν κεν … φεύγω is a conditional with the subjunctive φεύγω (for φεύγῳ), ‘if I flee’; ὑπὸ κρατεροῦ Ἀχιλῆος is ‘from under strong Achilles’, ‘before’ him. τῇ περ is ‘by the very way that’. ἀτυζόμενοι ‘dazed with fear’ goes with κλονέονται, the passive present of κλονέω, ‘are being thrown into confusion’. αἱρήσει (future of αἱρέω) με is ‘will take me’, καὶ ὧς ‘even so, all the same’, and δειροτομήσει ‘will cut the throat of’ (from δειρή ‘throat’ and τέμνω ‘cut’). ἀνάλκιδα is accusative, agreeing with με: ‘without might’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἂν ἐγὼ τούτους μὲν ὑποκλονέεσθαι ἐάσω
Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ, ποσὶν δ’ ἀπὸ τείχεος ἄλλῃ
φεύγω πρὸς πεδίον Ἰλήϊον, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκωμαι
Ἴδης τε κνημοὺς κατά τε ῥωπήϊα δύω·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ an egō toutous men hypokloneesthai easō
Pēleïdēi Achilēï, posin d’ apo teicheos allēi
pheugō pros pedion Ilēïon, ophr’ an hikōmai
Idēs te knēmous kata te rhōpēïa dyō·
sentences.l:
But if I, these men indeed, to be thrown into confusion allow
by Peleus’-son Achilles, and with my feet, away from the wall, elsewhere
I flee toward the Ilian plain, until I come to
the wooded slopes of Ida and sink down into the brushwood;
sentences.i: But suppose I let these men be thrown into confusion by Peleus’ son Achilles, and run on foot away from the wall in another direction, to the Ilian plain, until I reach the wooded slopes of Ida and sink down into the brushwood;
sentences.n: The second course: flee another way. εἰ … ἂν … ἐάσω is ‘if I let’, an aorist subjunctive of ἐάω ‘allow’, with τούτους ‘these men’ (the other Trojans), the rare compound ὑποκλονέεσθαι ‘to be driven in confusion’, and the dative Πηλεΐδῃ Ἀχιλῆϊ ‘by Peleus’ son Achilles’. ποσίν is ‘with my feet’, ἄλλῃ ‘elsewhere, in another direction’. Ἰλήϊον is an adjective from Ἴλος or Ἴλιος, ‘of Ilus’ or ‘of Ilium’; ‘Ilian’ is kept. ὄφρ’ ἂν ἵκωμαι is ‘until I reach’; the genitive Ἴδης (Ida) goes with κνημούς ‘wooded slopes’. ῥωπήϊα is ‘brushwood’, and κατά … δύω is tmesis, ‘sink down into’ (καταδύω), δύω being the aorist subjunctive after the same ὄφρ’ ἂν.

sentences.t:
ἑσπέριος δ’ ἂν ἔπειτα λοεσσάμενος ποταμοῖο
ἱδρῶ ἀποψυχθεὶς προτὶ Ἴλιον ἀπονεοίμην·
sentences.tr:
hesperios d’ an epeita loessamenos potamoio
hidrō apopsychtheis proti Ilion aponeoimēn·
sentences.l:
and at evening, then, having washed in the river,
my sweat cooled off, toward Ilium I might go back;
sentences.i: then at evening, when I had bathed in the river and cooled off my sweat, I could go back toward Ilium;
sentences.n: The rest of the second course: it would end well. ἑσπέριος ‘at evening’ is an adjective used as an adverb, and ἂν … ἀπονεοίμην ‘I could go back’ is an optative with ἄν, the answer to the ‘if’ clause above. λοεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of λούω ‘wash’, with the genitive ποταμοῖο ‘in the river’; ἱδρῶ is the accusative of ἱδρώς ‘sweat’, and ἀποψυχθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀποψύχω, ‘having cooled off’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός;
sentences.tr: alla ti ē moi tauta philos dielexato thymos;
sentences.l: But why indeed has my dear heart talked these things over with me?
sentences.i: But why has my own heart talked all this over with me?
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ τί ἤ (= ἦ) is ‘but why, indeed?’: he turns on his own plan, as Odysseus does with the same line at 11.407. διελέξατο is the aorist middle of διαλέγομαι, ‘talked through, talked over’, with ταῦτα ‘these things’ and μοι ‘with me’. φίλος … θυμός is ‘my dear heart’, φίλος being ‘own’.

sentences.t:
μή μ’ ἀπαειρόμενον πόλιος πεδίον δὲ νοήσῃ
καί με μεταΐξας μάρψῃ ταχέεσσι πόδεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
mē m’ apaeiromenon polios pedion de noēsēi
kai me metaïxas marpsēi tacheessi podessin.
sentences.l:
lest me, setting out from the city to the plain, he perceive,
and rushing after me seize me with his swift feet.
sentences.i: lest he see me setting out from the city for the plain, and dash after me and seize me with his swift feet.
sentences.n: Why the second course will not do. μή with the subjunctive νοήσῃ is the construction of fear, ‘lest he notice’. ἀπαειρόμενον is the present participle middle of ἀπαείρω, ‘lifting myself away, setting out’; πόλιος is the genitive ‘from the city’, and πεδίον δέ is ‘to the plain’ (-δε of motion). μεταΐξας is the aorist participle of μεταΐσσω ‘dash after’, and μάρψῃ the aorist subjunctive ‘seize’. ταχέεσσι is the epic dative plural in -εσσι(ν).

sentences.t:
οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ ἔσται θάνατον καὶ κῆρας ἀλύξαι·
λίην γὰρ κρατερὸς περὶ πάντων ἔστ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr:
ouket’ epeit’ estai thanaton kai kēras alyxai·
liēn gar krateros peri pantōn est’ anthrōpōn.
sentences.l:
No longer then will it be possible to escape death and the death-fates;
for exceedingly strong beyond all men he is.
sentences.i: There will then be no more escaping death and the fates of death; for he is exceedingly strong, beyond all men.
sentences.n: οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ ἔσται … ἀλύξαι is ‘it will no longer then be possible to escape’, ἔσται with the aorist infinitive of ἀλύσκω. θάνατον καὶ κῆρας is ‘death and the death-fates’; κήρ ‘death-fate’ is a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’. λίην is ‘exceedingly’, κρατερός ‘strong’, and περὶ πάντων … ἀνθρώπων ‘beyond all men’. ἔστ’ is ἐστί.

sentences.t: εἰ δέ κέ οἱ προπάροιθε πόλεος κατεναντίον ἔλθω·
sentences.tr: ei de ke hoi proparoithe poleos katenantion elthō·
sentences.l: But if, in front of the city, face to face with him I go;
sentences.i: But if I go out to face him in front of the city;
sentences.n: The third course: stand and fight. εἰ δέ κε … ἔλθω is ‘but if I go’, a subjunctive, and the sentence is never finished; what follows gives a reason it might work. οἱ is ‘him’ with κατεναντίον ‘face to face’, and προπάροιθε ‘in front of’ takes the genitive πόλεος (Ionic for πόλεως). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ θην τούτῳ τρωτὸς χρὼς ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
ἐν δὲ ἴα ψυχή, θνητὸν δέ ἕ φασ’ ἄνθρωποι
ἔμμεναι·
sentences.tr:
kai gar thēn toutōi trōtos chrōs oxeï chalkōi,
en de ia psychē, thnēton de he phas’ anthrōpoi
emmenai·
sentences.i: for this man’s skin can be wounded by sharp bronze, and there is but one life in him, and men say that he is mortal;
sentences.n: Why the third course might work. καὶ γάρ θην is ‘for indeed, surely’. τρωτός ‘woundable’ (from τιτρώσκω ‘wound’) goes with χρώς ‘skin’, and ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is the dative of means ‘by sharp bronze’. ἐν δὲ ἴα ψυχή is ‘and in him one life’: ἴα is the feminine ‘one’ (Attic μία), ψυχή the breath of life that leaves a dying man, and the verb ‘is’ is left out. θνητὸν δέ ἕ is ‘and him mortal’, φασ’ is φασι ‘they say’, and the infinitive ἔμμεναι (= εἶναι) opens the next line, so the unit runs on to it.

sentences.t: αὐτάρ οἱ Κρονίδης Ζεὺς κῦδος ὀπάζει.
sentences.tr: autar hoi Kronidēs Zeus kydos opazei.
sentences.l: but to him Zeus, the son of Cronus, glory grants.”
sentences.i: but Zeus, the son of Cronus, grants him glory.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ sets the god’s favour against the mortal body just described. οἱ is ‘to him’, Achilles; Κρονίδης Ζεύς is ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’. ὀπάζει ‘grants’ comes from ὀπάζω ‘make follow’, so the glory is made to attend him. κῦδος ‘glory’ is what Achilles was eager to win at 543. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν Ἀχιλῆα ἀλεὶς μένεν, ἐν δέ οἱ ἦτορ
ἄλκιμον ὁρμᾶτο πτολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn Achilēa aleis menen, en de hoi ētor
alkimon hormato ptolemizein ēde machesthai.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, Achilles, crouching, he awaited, and in him his heart
valiant was urged on to make war and to fight.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and crouching he waited for Achilles, and his valiant heart was stirred in him to make war and to fight.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ ends Agenor’s soliloquy. ἀλείς is the aorist passive participle of εἴλω (the verb of ἀλέντες at 534), ‘drawn together’, ‘crouching’. μένεν (= ἔμενε) is ‘awaited’, with the accusative Ἀχιλῆα. ἐν … οἱ is ‘in him’, ἄλκιμον ‘valiant’ agrees with ἦτορ ‘heart’, and ὁρμᾶτο is the imperfect of ὁρμάομαι, ‘was urged on’. πτολεμίζειν (= πολεμίζειν) is ‘make war’ and ἠδὲ ‘and’. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε πάρδαλις εἶσι βαθείης ἐκ ξυλόχοιο
ἀνδρὸς θηρητῆρος ἐναντίον, οὐδέ τι θυμῷ
ταρβεῖ οὐδὲ φοβεῖται, ἐπεί κεν ὑλαγμὸν ἀκούσῃ·
sentences.tr:
ēÿte pardalis eisi batheiēs ek xylochoio
andros thērētēros enantion, oude ti thymōi
tarbei oude phobeitai, epei ken hylagmon akousēi·
sentences.i: As a leopard comes out of a deep lair to face a hunter, and is not at all afraid in her heart or frightened when she hears the barking;
sentences.n: A simile for Agenor: the leopard. ἠΰτε is ‘as’. πάρδαλις is a feminine noun, ‘leopard’, and εἶσι the present of εἶμι ‘go’. ξύλοχος is the ‘lair’ or thicket where an animal lies, and ἐναντίον takes the genitive ἀνδρὸς θηρητῆρος, ‘against a man, a hunter’. ταρβεῖ is ‘is afraid’ (ταρβέω) and φοβεῖται ‘is frightened’. ἐπεί κεν … ἀκούσῃ is ‘when she has heard’; ὑλαγμός is ‘barking’, the dogs being left unnamed. The unit ends at an ano teleia, and the simile goes on.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γὰρ φθάμενός μιν ἢ οὐτάσῃ ἠὲ βάλῃσιν,
ἀλλά τε καὶ περὶ δουρὶ πεπαρμένη οὐκ ἀπολήγει
ἀλκῆς, πρίν γ’ ἠὲ ξυμβλήμεναι ἠὲ δαμῆναι·
sentences.tr:
ei per gar phthamenos min ē outasēi ēe balēisin,
alla te kai peri douri peparmenē ouk apolēgei
alkēs, prin g’ ēe xymblēmenai ēe damēnai·
sentences.i: For even if the hunter, striking first, either stabs her or hits her, still, pierced through on the spear, she does not give up her might before she has either closed with him or been overcome;
sentences.n: The leopard fights on even when speared. φθάμενος is the aorist participle of φθάνω, ‘getting in first’, and the hunter is the subject of οὐτάσῃ ‘stabs’ (a wound at close quarters) and βάλῃσιν ‘hits’, both subjunctives, ἢ … ἠέ ‘either … or’. πεπαρμένη is the perfect passive participle of πείρω ‘pierce’, ‘transfixed’, with περὶ δουρί ‘on the spear’. ἀπολήγει takes the genitive ἀλκῆς, ‘cease from might’. πρίν γ’ ἠὲ … ἠέ is ‘before either … or’, with the infinitives ξυμβλήμεναι ‘to close with’ (of συμβάλλω) and δαμῆναι ‘to be overcome’.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἀντήνορος υἱὸς ἀγαυοῦ δῖος Ἀγήνωρ
οὐκ ἔθελεν φεύγειν, πρὶν πειρήσαιτ’ Ἀχιλῆος.
sentences.tr:
hōs Antēnoros huios agauou dios Agēnōr
ouk ethelen pheugein, prin peirēsait’ Achilēos.
sentences.l:
so the son of noble Antenor, heavenly Agenor,
was not willing to flee, before he made trial of Achilles.
sentences.i: So the son of noble Antenor, heavenly Agenor, was unwilling to flee before he had made trial of Achilles.
sentences.n: The simile closes: ὣς ‘so’. The name is Ἀγήνωρ in the nominative, Ἀγήνορα in the accusative (545). ἀγαυός is ‘noble’. ἔθελεν is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘be willing’, and πρὶν πειρήσαιτ’ is πρίν with the aorist optative middle of πειράω, ‘before he had tried’, with the genitive Ἀχιλῆος.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ ἀσπίδα μὲν πρόσθ’ ἔσχετο πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην,
ἐγχείῃ δ’ αὐτοῖο τιτύσκετο, καὶ μέγ’ ἀΰτει·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho g’ ar’ aspida men prosth’ escheto pantos’ eïsēn,
encheiēi d’ autoio titysketo, kai meg’ aÿtei·
sentences.l:
but he then the shield before him held, equal on every side,
and with his spear at him took aim, and loudly shouted:
sentences.i: but he held his shield, equal on every side, before him, and took aim at him with his spear, and shouted aloud:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ is ‘but he then’. ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘held (before himself)’, and ἀσπίδα … πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην is ‘a shield equal on every side’, that is round. ἐγχείῃ is the dative of ἐγχείη ‘spear’, and τιτύσκετο takes the genitive αὐτοῖο (= αὐτοῦ), ‘aimed at him’. ἀΰτει is the imperfect of ἀϋτέω ‘shout’, without augment. His words follow.

sentences.t:
ἦ δή που μάλ’ ἔολπας ἐνὶ φρεσὶ φαίδιμ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
ἤματι τῷδε πόλιν πέρσειν Τρώων ἀγερώχων
νηπύτι’·
sentences.tr:
ē dē pou mal’ eolpas eni phresi phaidim’ Achilleu
ēmati tōide polin persein Trōōn agerōchōn
nēpyti’·
sentences.i: “Surely you now greatly hope, I suppose, in your wits, glorious Achilles, to sack the city of the lofty Trojans on this day, you child.
sentences.n: Agenor taunts Achilles. ἦ δή που is ‘surely now, I suppose’, with a bite of irony. ἔολπας is the perfect of ἔλπομαι, ‘you hope, expect’, and ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in your wits’. φαίδιμ’ is the vocative of φαίδιμος ‘glorious’. πέρσειν is the future infinitive of πέρθω ‘sack’. ἀγερώχων ‘lofty’ is the old guess at a word whose meaning is not known. νηπύτι’ (= νηπύτιε) is a scolding vocative, ‘you child’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἦ τ’ ἔτι πολλὰ τετεύξεται ἄλγε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῇ.
sentences.tr: ē t’ eti polla teteuxetai alge’ ep’ autēi.
sentences.l: truly yet many pains will be wrought over it.
sentences.i: Truly, many pains will still be wrought over it.
sentences.n: ἦ τ’ ἔτι is ‘truly yet’. τετεύξεται is the future perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, here simply ‘will be wrought’, with πολλὰ ἄλγεα ‘many pains’ (ἄλγε’ is elided), and ἐπ’ αὐτῇ is ‘over it, about it’, the city. The meaning is that taking the city will cost Achilles dear.

sentences.t:
ἐν γάρ οἱ πολέες τε καὶ ἄλκιμοι ἀνέρες εἰμέν,
οἳ καὶ πρόσθε φίλων τοκέων ἀλόχων τε καὶ υἱῶν
Ἴλιον εἰρυόμεσθα·
sentences.tr:
en gar hoi polees te kai alkimoi aneres eimen,
hoi kai prosthe philōn tokeōn alochōn te kai huiōn
Ilion eiryomestha·
sentences.i: for there are many of us in it, and valiant men, who guard Ilium in defence of our dear parents, our wives, and our sons;
sentences.n: ἐν γάρ οἱ is ‘for in it’, οἱ being the city. εἰμέν is the epic first plural of εἰμί (= ἐσμέν), and πολέες the epic πολλοί. πρόσθε takes the genitives φίλων τοκέων ἀλόχων τε καὶ υἱῶν, ‘in front of, in defence of’ parents, wives and sons. εἰρυόμεσθα (= ἐρυόμεθα) is ‘we guard’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἐνθάδε πότμον ἐφέψεις
ὧδ’ ἔκπαγλος ἐὼν καὶ θαρσαλέος πολεμιστής.
sentences.tr:
sy d’ enthade potmon ephepseis
hōd’ ekpaglos eōn kai tharsaleos polemistēs.
sentences.l:
but you here your doom will come upon,
being so terrifying and a bold warrior.”
sentences.i: but you will meet your doom here, terrifying as you are, and a bold warrior.”
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ ‘but you’ answers the ‘we’ of the last unit. ἐφέψεις is the future of ἐφέπω ‘go after’, which with πότμον ‘doom’ is ‘come upon, meet’. ὧδ’ is ὧδε ‘so’, ἔκπαγλος ‘terrifying’, and ἐών is the epic participle (= ὤν) of εἰμί. θαρσαλέος ‘bold’ comes from θάρσος ‘courage’ (the word of 547). The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ὀξὺν ἄκοντα βαρείης χειρὸς ἀφῆκε,
καί ῥ’ ἔβαλε κνήμην ὑπὸ γούνατος οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτεν.
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai oxyn akonta bareiēs cheiros aphēke,
kai rh’ ebale knēmēn hypo gounatos oud’ aphamarten.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and the sharp javelin from his heavy hand let go,
and struck the shin below the knee, and did not miss.
sentences.i: So he said, and let fly the sharp javelin from his heavy hand, and struck the shin below the knee, and did not miss.
sentences.n: Agenor’s throw. ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’ is the formula that turns from speech to action. ὀξὺν ἄκοντα is ‘the sharp javelin’, a missile for throwing, and βαρείης χειρός is the genitive ‘from his heavy hand’ (βαρύς ‘heavy’). ἀφῆκε is the aorist of ἀφίημι ‘let go, let fly’. κνήμην ὑπὸ γούνατος is ‘the shin below the knee’, and οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτεν ‘and did not miss’ is the aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω. A new paragraph begins.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κνημὶς νεοτεύκτου κασσιτέροιο
σμερδαλέον κονάβησε·
sentences.tr:
amphi de hoi knēmis neoteuktou kassiteroio
smerdaleon konabēse·
sentences.l:
And about him the greave of newly worked tin
rang terribly;
sentences.i: and the greave of newly worked tin rang terribly about him;
sentences.n: The greave is Achilles’. ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ is ‘and about him’, with ἀμφί as an adverb. κνημίς is the ‘greave’, a shin-guard, and νεοτεύκτου κασσιτέροιο ‘of newly worked tin’ has the genitive -οιο (= -ου). κονάβησε ‘rang’ is the aorist of κοναβέω, and σμερδαλέον ‘terribly’ is a neuter accusative used as an adverb. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
πάλιν δ’ ἀπὸ χαλκὸς ὄρουσε
βλημένου, οὐδ’ ἐπέρησε, θεοῦ δ’ ἠρύκακε δῶρα.
sentences.tr:
palin d’ apo chalkos orouse
blēmenou, oud’ eperēse, theou d’ ērykake dōra.
sentences.l:
and back from the struck one the bronze leapt away,
and did not pierce, and the god’s gifts held it off.
sentences.i: and the bronze leapt back off the man it had struck, and did not pierce him, for the gifts of the god held it off.
sentences.n: The spearhead (χαλκός ‘bronze’) rebounds. ὄρουσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, here intransitive ‘leapt’. βλημένου is the aorist participle of βάλλω in the genitive, ‘of the man hit’, after ἀπό. ἐπέρησε is ‘pierced’. ἠρύκακε is the reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and its subject is the neuter plural δῶρα ‘gifts’ with a singular verb; θεοῦ δῶρα is ‘the gifts of a god’, Achilles’ armour, the god not being named here.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ὁρμήσατ’ Ἀγήνορος ἀντιθέοιο
δεύτερος·
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs d’ hormēsat’ Agēnoros antitheoio
deuteros·
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son rushed upon Agenor, godlike,
second;
sentences.i: Then in his turn Peleus’ son rushed upon godlike Agenor;
sentences.n: Now it is Achilles’ turn. Πηλεΐδης is the patronymic ‘Peleus’-son’. ὁρμήσατ’ is ὁρμήσατο, the aorist middle of ὁρμάω ‘rush’, with the genitive Ἀγήνορος ‘upon Agenor’. δεύτερος is ‘second’, that is ‘next, in his turn’, since Agenor threw first. ἀντιθέοιο ‘godlike’ has the genitive -οιο (= -ου).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔασεν Ἀπόλλων κῦδος ἀρέσθαι,
ἀλλά μιν ἐξήρπαξε, κάλυψε δ’ ἄρ’ ἠέρι πολλῇ,
ἡσύχιον δ’ ἄρα μιν πολέμου ἔκπεμπε νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ et’ easen Apollōn kydos aresthai,
alla min exērpaxe, kalypse d’ ar’ ēeri pollēi,
hēsychion d’ ara min polemou ekpempe neesthai.
sentences.l:
nor any longer did Apollo allow glory to be won,
but snatched him away, and covered him then with thick mist,
and quietly sent him out of the war to go.
sentences.i: But Apollo no longer allowed him to win glory: he snatched Agenor away, covered him in thick mist, and quietly sent him out of the war to go.
sentences.n: Apollo rescues Agenor. οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔασεν is ‘no longer allowed’ (ἔασεν the aorist of ἐάω), and the one who would have won κῦδος ‘glory’ (the aorist infinitive middle ἀρέσθαι) is Achilles, left unnamed. ἐξήρπαξε is the aorist of ἐξαρπάζω ‘snatch away’, and ἠέρι πολλῇ is ‘thick mist’. ἡσύχιον ‘quietly’ is a neuter accusative used as an adverb, πολέμου ‘out of the war’ a genitive of separation after ἔκπεμπε ‘was sending out’, and νέεσθαι ‘to go’ (= νεῖσθαι) an infinitive of purpose.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ Πηλεΐωνα δόλῳ ἀποέργαθε λαοῦ·
sentences.tr: autar ho Pēleïōna dolōi apoergathe laou·
sentences.l: but he, Peleus’-son, with a trick kept away from the people;
sentences.i: but he kept the son of Peleus away from the people by a trick;
sentences.n: ὃ is Apollo, and Πηλεΐωνα, accusative, is Achilles, a second patronymic form, ‘Peleus’-son’. ἀποέργαθε is a past tense of ἀπείργω ‘keep away from’, without augment, with the genitive λαοῦ ‘from the people’, here the Trojans flooding to the city. δόλῳ is ‘by a trick’, a dative of means, and the trick is told in the next lines.

sentences.t:
αὐτῷ γὰρ ἑκάεργος Ἀγήνορι πάντα ἐοικὼς
ἔστη πρόσθε ποδῶν, ὃ δ’ ἐπέσσυτο ποσσὶ διώκειν·
sentences.tr:
autōi gar hekaergos Agēnori panta eoikōs
estē prosthe podōn, ho d’ epessyto possi diōkein·
sentences.l:
for to Agenor himself the far-working one, in everything like,
stood in front of his feet, and he rushed on with his feet to pursue;
sentences.i: for the god who works from afar, made like Agenor himself in everything, stood before his feet, and he rushed on to chase him on foot;
sentences.n: The trick: Apollo takes Agenor’s shape. ἑκάεργος stands for the god’s name; its meaning is disputed (‘far-working’ or ‘far-shooting’). αὐτῷ … Ἀγήνορι with ἐοικώς, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, is ‘made like Agenor himself’, and πάντα is ‘in everything’. ἔστη πρόσθε ποδῶν is ‘stood in front of his feet’, right before Achilles. ὃ δ’ is Achilles; ἐπέσσυτο is the aorist of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush on’, ποσσί the dative plural of πούς, ‘with his feet’, and διώκειν ‘to chase’.

sentences.t:
εἷος ὃ τὸν πεδίοιο διώκετο πυροφόροιο
τρέψας πὰρ ποταμὸν βαθυδινήεντα Σκάμανδρον
τυτθὸν ὑπεκπροθέοντα·
sentences.tr:
heios ho ton pedioio diōketo pyrophoroio
trepsas par potamon bathydinēenta Skamandron
tytthon hypekprotheonta·
sentences.i: While he was chasing him across the wheat-bearing plain, and had turned him toward the deep-eddying river Scamander, with the pursued running a little way ahead,
sentences.n: εἷος (= ἕως) is ‘while’; the clause runs to the ano teleia and the main verb ἔθελγεν comes in the next unit. ὃ is Achilles, τόν the false Agenor, and διώκετο an imperfect in a middle form with active sense, ‘was chasing’. τρέψας is the aorist participle of τρέπω ‘turn’, nominative and so agreeing with the chaser; the one turned toward the river is ‘him’, the pursued, and the English keeps the Greek’s words. πυροφόροιο is ‘wheat-bearing’, βαθυδινήεντα ‘deep-eddying’, τυτθόν ‘a little’, and ὑπεκπροθέοντα, a rare compound of ὑπό, ἐκ, πρό and θέω, ‘running out ahead’, agrees with τόν.

sentences.t:
δόλῳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔθελγεν Ἀπόλλων
ὡς αἰεὶ ἔλποιτο κιχήσεσθαι ποσὶν οἷσι·
sentences.tr:
dolōi d’ ar’ ethelgen Apollōn
hōs aiei elpoito kichēsesthai posin hoisi·
sentences.l:
and with a trick then enchanted him Apollo,
so that he might always hope to overtake him with his own feet;
sentences.i: and Apollo enchanted him with a trick, so that he kept hoping to catch him with his own feet;
sentences.n: δόλῳ ‘with a trick’; ἔθελγεν is the imperfect of θέλγω ‘enchant, charm’, here a charm worked by a trick. ὡς with the optative ἔλποιτο (ἔλπομαι ‘hope’) gives the purpose, ‘so that he kept hoping’, and αἰεί is ‘always’. κιχήσεσθαι is the future infinitive middle of κιχάνω ‘overtake’. ποσὶν οἷσι is ‘with his own feet’, οἷσι being the possessive ὅς, not the relative. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τόφρ’ ἄλλοι Τρῶες πεφοβημένοι ἦλθον ὁμίλῳ
ἀσπάσιοι προτὶ ἄστυ, πόλις δ’ ἔμπλητο ἀλέντων.
sentences.tr:
tophr’ alloi Trōes pephobēmenoi ēlthon homilōi
aspasioi proti asty, polis d’ emplēto alentōn.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the other Trojans, terrified, came in a throng,
glad, to the town, and the city was filled with those crowded together.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the rest of the Trojans, terrified, came to the town in a throng, glad to be there, and the city was filled with those who had crowded in together.
sentences.n: While Achilles is led off, the rest reach safety. τόφρ’ (= τόφρα) is ‘meanwhile’. πεφοβημένοι is the perfect participle of φοβέομαι, ‘terrified’, ὁμίλῳ ‘in a throng’ a dative, and ἀσπάσιοι ‘glad’, said of the Trojans at reaching the city. προτὶ ἄστυ is ‘to the town’. ἔμπλητο is an aorist of ἐμπίμπλημι in a middle form with passive sense, ‘was filled’, with the genitive ἀλέντων ‘with those crowded together’ (ἀλέντες as at 534).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα τοί γ’ ἔτλαν πόλιος καὶ τείχεος ἐκτὸς
μεῖναι ἔτ’ ἀλλήλους, καὶ γνώμεναι ὅς τε πεφεύγοι
ὅς τ’ ἔθαν’ ἐν πολέμῳ·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ara toi g’ etlan polios kai teicheos ektos
meinai et’ allēlous, kai gnōmenai hos te pepheugoi
hos t’ ethan’ en polemōi·
sentences.i: Nor did they dare to wait for one another any longer outside the city and the wall, and learn who had escaped and who had died in the war;
sentences.n: τοί γε ‘they’ are the Trojans. ἔτλαν is the aorist of τλάω ‘dare’, and ἐκτός ‘outside’ takes the genitives πόλιος καὶ τείχεος. μεῖναι is the aorist infinitive ‘to wait for’, with ἀλλήλους ‘one another’, and γνώμεναι the epic infinitive (= γνῶναι) ‘to find out’. ὅς τε … ὅς τ’ is ‘who … and who’: πεφεύγοι is the perfect optative of φεύγω, ‘had escaped’, and ἔθαν’ (= ἔθανε) the aorist of θνῄσκω, ‘had died’. The unit ends at an ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐσσυμένως ἐσέχυντο
ἐς πόλιν, ὅν τινα τῶν γε πόδες καὶ γοῦνα σαώσαι.
sentences.tr:
all’ essymenōs esechynto
es polin, hon tina tōn ge podes kai gouna saōsai.
sentences.l:
but hurriedly they poured
into the city, whomever of them his feet and knees might save.
sentences.i: but poured in haste into the city, every man whom his feet and knees might save.
sentences.n: ἐσσυμένως is ‘hurriedly’, and ἐσέχυντο is the aorist middle of εἰσχέω, ‘poured in’, the rout seen as a stream. ὅν τινα τῶν γε is ‘whomever of them’, with the optative σαώσαι (from σαόω ‘save’) in a general sense: whichever man’s feet and knees carried him. γοῦνα is the epic plural of γόνυ ‘knee’.
